content: The symptoms of eczema, such as intense itching, can significantly disrupt sleep and lead to fatigue, ultimately affecting the quality of life. The rationale for using oral H1 antihistamines (H1 AH) as an additional therapy alongside topical treatments is based on their ability to block histamine receptors in the skin, potentially reducing itching. This approach aims to enhance the anti-inflammatory effects of topical treatments. However, it is considered unethical to compare oral H1 AH alone to no treatment, as topical therapy is the standard care for eczema. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of oral H1 antihistamines as an adjunct to topical treatments in both adults and children with eczema. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oral H1 AH plus topical treatment to topical treatment with either placebo or no additional therapy. The primary outcomes assessed were changes in patient-reported eczema symptoms and the proportion of participants experiencing adverse effects or serious adverse events. Secondary outcomes included changes in physician-assessed clinical signs, quality of life, and the frequency of eczema flares. A total of 25 studies involving 3,285 participants were included. Of these, 17 studies focused on adults (1,344 participants), and 8 studies involved children (1,941 participants). Most studies did not report the baseline severity of eczema, but they were conducted in secondary care settings, suggesting that participants likely had more severe cases. The duration of the trials ranged from three days to 18 months, and 13 different H1 AH treatments were studied. Due to significant variability in study design, including differences in treatment duration, dosage, and outcome measures, pooling of data was not possible. The risk of bias was generally unclear, with five studies showing a high risk of bias in at least one domain (e.g., attrition, selection, or reporting bias). Only one study assessed quality of life, but the data were insufficient for statistical analysis. Cetirizine versus Placebo In one study involving 795 children, cetirizine (0.5 mg/kg/day) was compared to placebo over 18 months. The study did not separately report patient-assessed symptoms of eczema, such as itching. Cetirizine was associated with fewer adverse events, which were mostly mild (risk ratio [RR] 0.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.46 to 1.01). It also appeared to reduce the need for additional H1 AH use as an indicator of eczema flare rate (P = 0.035), although no further numerical data were provided. Physician-assessed clinical signs, measured using the SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) index, improved in both groups, but the difference between groups was not statistically significant. The evidence for this comparison was of moderate quality. Another study involving 84 adults compared cetirizine (10 mg/day) to placebo over four weeks. No significant differences were observed between groups in patient-assessed symptoms of eczema (pruritus measured as part of SCORAD), adverse events (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.50 to 2.45; mostly sedation, skin-related issues, respiratory symptoms, or headache), physician-assessed clinical signs, or the amount of rescue therapy required. The evidence for this comparison was of low quality. Fexofenadine versus Placebo One study involving 400 adults compared fexofenadine (120 mg/day) to placebo over one week. Fexofenadine likely resulted in a small reduction in patient-assessed pruritus on a scale of 0 to 8 (mean difference [MD] -0.25, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.07). It also led to a greater reduction in the ratio of physician-assessed pruritus area to total body surface area (P = 0.007), although these reductions may not be clinically meaningful. There was likely little or no difference in adverse events (mostly somnolence and headache) (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.50) or in the amount of 0.1% hydrocortisone butyrate used as an indicator of eczema flares. The evidence for this comparison was of moderate quality. Loratadine versus Placebo A study involving 28 adults compared loratadine (10 mg/day) to placebo over four weeks. No significant differences were found between groups in patient-assessed pruritus (measured using a 100-point visual analogue scale; MD -2.30, 95% CI -20.27 to 15.67), physician-assessed clinical signs (SCORAD; MD -4.10, 95% CI -13.22 to 5.02), or adverse events. Only one adverse event (folliculitis) was reported, which occurred in the placebo group (RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.01 to 5.76). The number of eczema flares was not measured in this study. The evidence for this comparison was of low quality. Authors' Conclusions The review did not find consistent evidence to support the effectiveness of H1 AH treatments as an adjunct to topical therapy for eczema when compared to placebo. The quality of evidence was generally low to moderate. Fexofenadine may provide a small improvement in patient-assessed pruritus, with no significant difference in the amount of treatment required to prevent eczema flares. Cetirizine showed no advantage over placebo in terms of physician-assessed clinical signs or patient-reported symptoms. Similarly, loratadine did not demonstrate any benefit over placebo. All interventions appeared to be safe. The quality of evidence was limited by poor study design and imprecise results. Future research should focus on clearly defining the condition (including its course and severity) and reporting methods, particularly participant selection, randomization, baseline characteristics, and outcomes, in line with the Harmonising Outcome Measures in Eczema (HOME) initiative.
